beliefs.practice: Use a single long-lived AsyncIOMotorClient instance (created once at app startup and closed on shutdown) instead of creating a client per request; configure the client with connection pool settings (e.g. maxPoolSize/minPoolSize) via the connection string or client kwargs.

Read the cluster connection string only from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime; never write the actual secret into source files, logs or checked-in fixtures — provide a .env.example with a placeholder instead.
For production secrets use a secret manager (Azure Key Vault) or managed identity rather than storing connection strings in plain .env files; load the secret at runtime from Key Vault when possible.
Require TLS/SSL for connections (tls=true / ssl=true or explicit TLS parameters) and verify server certificates; refuse non-TLS connections to the cluster.
Set client timeouts to avoid hung requests: set serverSelectionTimeoutMS (e.g. 5000 ms) and socketTimeoutMS appropriately in the connection string or client kwargs.

Enable (or implement) automatic retries with exponential backoff for transient network/availability errors and idempotent operations; prefer using driver-level retryWrites/retryReads where available plus an application-level retry wrapper for non-idempotent operations.

Pin Motor, PyMongo and Beanie to specific compatible versions in requirements.txt (explicit versions) to avoid runtime incompatibilities — verify Beanie's required PyMongo/Motor versions before install and test initialization locally.

Always specify the database name explicitly when creating the client or when calling beanie.init_beanie (use database='sample_retail_15') so the app only touches that database and not other databases on the cluster.

Create indexes for fields used in filters and group-by/aggregation steps: create an ascending index on supplier_id and a compound index on (supplier_id, status) to accelerate the open-PO-by-supplier aggregation.

Create a unique index on any business key (e.g. purchase_order_number) at collection creation time to enforce uniqueness and improve lookup performance; do index creation during app startup or a deploy/seed step, not on each request.

When designing the aggregation pipeline, $match as early as possible (filter first) then $group; use covered projections to return only required fields and use allowDiskUse=true for large aggregations if supported.

Enforce required fields both at the application layer (Pydantic/Beanie validators) and, where possible, with server-side schema validation (MongoDB JSON Schema validator) to protect against accidental writes from other clients.

Avoid multi-document transactions unless necessary; prefer modeling to reduce cross-document transactions, because distributed transactions add latency and complexity and may be limited in managed MongoDB-compatible services.

For vector search, create a vector index on the embedding field with explicit algorithm parameters (e.g. HNSW / efConstruction / M, or IVF params): declare field type and indexing params at collection/index creation time rather than via ad-hoc queries.

When using an ODM (Beanie), initialize Beanie exactly once with beanie.init_beanie(models=[...], database=db) during startup; ensure the Motor client passed matches the version expectations of Beanie to avoid runtime missing-method errors.

Provision indexes and any required collections as part of a seed/deploy script and validate their existence with an admin tool (the cluster's management console or 'mongo' client) rather than relying on first-write index creation in production.
Limit returned fields in CRUD endpoints (use projection) to minimize data transferred and to avoid leaking sensitive fields; return computed aggregation summaries only from dedicated endpoints.
Instrument and log query performance (explain plans) for heavy aggregation endpoints; verify the pipeline uses indexes by checking explain() and adjust indexes if aggregation is collection-scanning.

Configure request/operation-level limits (pagination, batch sizes, limit/skip avoidance) on list endpoints to prevent unbounded result scans; use range or index-based pagination instead of skip for large collections.

If the managed service bills by provisioned throughput (RUs), monitor and use autoscale where possible and avoid hot partitions; design partition key (for Mongo API this might be _id shard key/partitioning) to evenly distribute load across partitions.
